55477048f9.q: What percentage of new product launches at Coca-Cola met on-time, on-quality, and on-cost targets when Kimberly Williams first assessed the manufacturing process?
55477048f9.a: When Williams first focused on new product integration in manufacturing, she discovered that the organization was launching products on time in full with expected cost and quality less than 60 percent of the time, meaning there was a 40-point gap that needed to be recovered. Through value stream mapping and cross-functional collaboration with marketing, R&D, procurement, and finance, the team uncovered that the problem was not solely in manufacturing but distributed across multiple functions.
55477048f9.rq: Success has moved from personal achievement to impact through enabling others and leaving behind something sustainable.
ks: 60 percent: new product launch success rate (on-time, on-quality, on-cost) at Coca-Cola when Williams first assessed manufacturing
40-point gap: the percentage improvement needed in new product integration across manufacturing, R&D, procurement, marketing, and finance
10-15 points: the gap contribution from Research and Development delays in new product integration
10 points: the gap contribution from Procurement not being brought into the loop early enough
7 points: the gap closed within the first six months through pilot pit crews and cross-functional improvements
55477048f9.gt: Vice President of Syrup Manufacturing at Coca-Cola North America

85e0059a6e.q: What are Kimberly Williams' three universal leadership lessons from leading across 40+ sites in 11 countries?
85e0059a6e.a: Williams identified three main leadership lessons: first, what people need from their leaders is universal—they need to know if they matter and where the organization is going; second, listen before you lead, which means seeking out and soaking in local expertise rather than imposing a single way of doing things; and third, clarity is critical—people perform better when they understand where the organization is headed and their role in getting there, which Williams describes as her superpower of bringing clarity to chaos.

00a12d8a24.q: How did Kimberly Williams reduce the manufacturing gap in new product integration within the first six months through pilot pit crews?
00a12d8a24.a: Williams implemented pilot pit crews that improved regular production efficiencies, allowing the team to cut changeovers and move pilots more effectively and faster. This enabled frontline operators to be involved and understand the end-to-end vision of new products, while more intentionally leveraging pilot information to improve cost and quality. The manufacturing team was able to close seven points of the original 40-point gap within the first six months.

bbfc877848.q: What career transition did Kimberly Williams make from marketing to manufacturing, and what prompted it?
bbfc877848.a: Williams moved from marketing and new product development into manufacturing on a dare after a frustrated plant engineer challenged her to prove she could do better when she questioned whether the manufacturing team would get a launch right. Though not a recommended career strategy, this move proved transformative because it allowed her to lead a large team of people for the first time and gain exposure to lean manufacturing and continuous improvement culture, ultimately sparking her lifelong passion for manufacturing.

314978c13c.q: How has Kimberly Williams' definition of success evolved throughout her career in manufacturing leadership?
314978c13c.a: Williams' definition of success has evolved from personal achievement to impact through enabling others and leaving behind something sustainable. She explains that if everything depends on her, she hasn't really built anyone else or anything sustainable, so today she focuses much more on what she can enable others to accomplish and continually seeks feedback from her teams to improve her leadership effectiveness.
